title: Rails Across America
summary: America was huge, and horses were slow, so Americans built railroads of their own. A tiny engine called Tom Thumb raced a horse (and lost when a belt slipped!), and soon American trains had cowcatchers, bells and swivelling wheels for curvy tracks. During the Civil War, trains carried soldiers, and President Lincoln signed a law to build a railroad all the way to the Pacific.

sections.heading: A Huge Country, a Slow Way to Cross It
paragraphs: Picture the United States in the 1820s. It was a young country, only about fifty years old, and it was enormous. Most Americans lived near the Atlantic coast, but settlers were pushing west across the Appalachian Mountains towards the Ohio River and the great valley of the Mississippi. Between the farms of the west and the ports of the east lay hundreds of miles of forest, hills and rough dirt roads.

Moving things across that distance was painfully slow. A farmer in Ohio could grow a fine crop of wheat or corn, but hauling it east by wagon could cost more than the crop was worth. For most of history, the speed of a journey over land had been set by the speed of a horse.

Then, in 1825, the State of New York opened the Erie Canal, a man-made waterway about 580 km (363 miles) long that joined the Hudson River to the Great Lakes. Suddenly, goods from the west could float all the way to New York City cheaply. New York boomed. Other port cities watched with alarm. If all the trade of the west poured into New York, what would happen to them?

One of the most worried cities was Baltimore, in Maryland. Baltimore was a busy port, but it had no easy water route to the west, because mountains stood in the way and a canal over them would be fantastically difficult. Some Baltimore merchants had been reading news from England, where the Stockton and Darlington Railway had opened in 1825 and engineers were arguing about locomotives. Perhaps, they thought, a railway could do what a canal could not.

Americans were watching British experiments closely. In 1829 an engineer named Horatio Allen ran a British-built locomotive called the Stourbridge Lion on a coal company track at Honesdale, Pennsylvania. It was one of the first steam locomotives ever to run in America, but it was too heavy for the light wooden track, and it never went into regular service.

So America began by borrowing British ideas. But very soon, American engineers would discover that their country needed trains of its own design. Their land was wider, wilder and cheaper; their money was scarcer; and their tracks would have to wiggle around hills instead of tunnelling straight through them. The story of American railways is the story of taking a British invention and reshaping it for a whole continent.

sections.heading: A First Stone on the Fourth of July
paragraphs: In February 1827 the State of Maryland granted a charter, a legal permission to exist and to build, to a brand new company: the Baltimore and Ohio Rail Road. Virginia agreed a few weeks later. The plan was breathtakingly bold. The company would build a railway all the way from Baltimore over the Appalachian Mountains to the Ohio River, hundreds of miles away. At the time, nobody in America had ever built anything like it.

The founders chose a very special day to start. On 4 July 1828, the 52nd birthday of the United States, a huge crowd gathered in Baltimore for a parade with bands, banners and marching tradesmen. The guest of honour was a man of about 90 named Charles Carroll of Carrollton. Carroll was the last living person who had signed the Declaration of Independence in 1776. He lifted a spade and helped set the first stone of the new railroad. He is said to have remarked that he considered this one of the most important acts of his life, second only to signing the Declaration. Whether he used exactly those words is hard to prove, but the meaning of the day was clear: the old revolution was handing the future to a new one.

Building the line was slow and expensive. The B and O's engineers had very little experience, so they learned as they went. Some of the early track was made of stone blocks or wooden rails topped with thin strips of iron. Workers dug cuttings, built embankments and put up handsome stone bridges. One of them, the Thomas Viaduct at Relay, Maryland, was finished in 1835. Its graceful curve of stone arches made it the longest bridge in the United States at the time, and amazingly it still carries trains today.

The first section of line opened on 24 May 1830. It ran about 13 miles (21 km) west from Baltimore to Ellicott's Mills, a mill town on the Patapsco River now called Ellicott City. Passengers could ride there and back for a day out. But here is a surprise: those first B and O trains were pulled by horses. The company was not yet sure that steam locomotives would work on its sharply curving track, and some directors even experimented with a car pushed by a sail and with a horse walking on a treadmill inside a car.

The B and O kept pushing west for more than twenty years. It finally reached the Ohio River in 1852 and the city of Wheeling, in what is now West Virginia, on 1 January 1853. By then it had become one of the most important railroads in America. But in 1830, the company still had to be convinced that steam was the answer. That job fell to a small, noisy engine with a funny name.

sections.heading: Tom Thumb and the Great Race
paragraphs: Peter Cooper was a New York businessman and inventor who had bought land in Baltimore and badly wanted the railroad to succeed. Many experts claimed that locomotives could never manage the B and O's tight curves. Cooper believed they were wrong, and in 1829 he decided to prove it by building a little locomotive himself.

He called it Tom Thumb, after the tiny hero of an old English fairy tale, because it was so small. Cooper had to improvise with whatever parts he could find. His boiler stood upright, rather than lying on its side as in British engines, and according to the well-known story its boiler tubes were made from old rifle barrels. A single vertical cylinder drove the wheels. To make the fire burn hot enough in such a small boiler, Cooper added a fan, called a blower, that was turned by a belt from the wheels and blasted air into the fire. Tom Thumb was built as a demonstration machine, never meant to carry paying passengers day after day.

In the summer of 1830 Tom Thumb pulled an open car crowded with B and O directors out to Ellicott's Mills and back. Then came the most famous moment in its short life. On the return trip, at a place called the Relay House, a stagecoach company had brought a fine grey horse pulling a car on the parallel track. A race was arranged back towards Baltimore, a run of about 8 miles (13 km). Most historians date it to late August 1830, though old sources disagree about the exact day.

At first the horse jumped ahead, because a horse can reach full speed in a few strides while a steam engine needs time to build up. But once Tom Thumb got going it caught up, drew level and pulled ahead while the passengers cheered. Then disaster struck. The belt that drove the blower slipped off its pulley. Without the fan, the fire died down, the boiler lost pressure and the little engine slowed to a crawl. The horse trotted past and won the race.

So the horse won. But the people watching understood what they had seen. A tiny, home-made engine had outrun a strong horse until a simple belt failed, and a belt is easy to fix. The B and O's leaders were convinced. In 1831 the company held its own contest for American-built locomotives, and soon afterwards it stopped using horses on its main line. The original Tom Thumb did not survive, but in 1927 the B and O built a working replica for its 100th birthday celebration, the Fair of the Iron Horse. That replica can still be seen at the B and O Railroad Museum in Baltimore.

sections.heading: The Best Friend of Charleston
paragraphs: While Baltimore argued about horses and steam, another port city in the South was making its own move. Charleston, in South Carolina, was worried that cotton from inland farms was being shipped down rivers to rival ports instead of coming to its own wharves. So its merchants backed the South Carolina Canal and Rail Road Company, which planned a line inland to the town of Hamburg on the Savannah River.

This company made a bold decision right from the start: it would use steam locomotives, not horses. For its first engine it ordered a locomotive from the West Point Foundry in New York City. The engine arrived in Charleston by ship in October 1830 and was given a wonderful name: the Best Friend of Charleston. It is widely regarded as the first locomotive built entirely in the United States for regular, paying service.

On Christmas Day, 25 December 1830, the Best Friend pulled its first run with passengers aboard, and soon it was running a regular service on the first few miles of the line, about 6 miles (10 km) of track. This was the first regularly scheduled steam-powered passenger train service in the United States. The engine could pull several cars at around 15 to 25 miles per hour (about 25 to 40 km/h), faster than any horse could keep up for long. For the people of Charleston, a ride behind the puffing machine was a thrilling new adventure.

Sadly, the Best Friend's career was short. On 17 June 1831 its boiler exploded. According to accounts of the accident, the fireman, the worker who tended the fire, was annoyed by the hiss of steam escaping from the safety valve. The safety valve is the part that lets out steam when pressure gets too high, so that the boiler cannot burst. The fireman is said to have held the valve shut, or tied it down, to stop the noise. With nowhere to escape, the pressure rose and rose until the boiler blew apart. The fireman was badly injured and died; the engineer, Nicholas Darrell, survived.

It was the first locomotive boiler explosion in the United States, and it taught a hard lesson. Safety devices only work if nobody interferes with them. The railroad brought in stricter rules about who could touch the engine's controls. It also came up with a clever way to calm nervous passengers: for a while, a flat wagon piled with bales of cotton was placed between the locomotive and the passenger cars, as a cushion in case of another explosion.

The Best Friend's surviving parts were used to build a new engine with a very fitting name: the Phoenix, after the mythical bird that rises again from the ashes. And the railroad kept growing. When its line to Hamburg was finished in 1833, it ran about 136 miles (219 km), which made it, for a short time, one of the longest railways in the world. A replica of the Best Friend, built in 1928, still exists today, and Charleston has a small museum telling its story.

sections.heading: Making the Locomotive American
paragraphs: British railways were built like fortresses. Britain was a small, crowded and wealthy country, so its engineers could afford heavy rails, gentle curves, deep cuttings, long tunnels and fences along the line. American railroads had the opposite situation: endless distances, very little money and plenty of cheap land and timber. So American builders laid light track as fast and cheaply as they could, let it curve sharply around hills instead of cutting through them, and often left it unfenced. British-style locomotives, with their wheels fixed rigidly in a stiff frame, found such track very hard going. They bumped, rocked and sometimes jumped the rails.

The answer was one of the most important railway inventions ever made: the swivelling front truck, also called a bogie. In 1832 John B. Jervis, chief engineer of the Mohawk and Hudson Railroad in New York, built a locomotive called the Experiment whose front end rested on a small four-wheeled cart that could pivot underneath it. When the track curved, the little truck turned first and guided the rest of the engine smoothly into the bend, a bit like the front wheels of a shopping trolley swinging around a corner. The truck also spread the engine's weight over more wheels, which was gentler on flimsy rails. Locomotives with a four-wheel front truck and one pair of big driving wheels became known as the Jervis type, and the swivelling truck soon spread everywhere. Look under almost any train carriage today, anywhere in the world, and you will see bogies.

The John Bull shows the transformation clearly. It was built by Robert Stephenson and Company in Newcastle in 1831, shipped across the ocean in crates to the Camden and Amboy Railroad in New Jersey, and put together by a young mechanic named Isaac Dripps without any instructions. The Camden and Amboy Railroad's mechanics added a leading truck to help it cope with rough track. Isaac Dripps also fitted it with a pilot, a frame of sloping bars sticking out at the front. Its nickname tells you what it was for: the cowcatcher. On unfenced American lines, cattle, deer, fallen branches and other obstacles often wandered or tumbled onto the track. The pilot was shaped to push anything it hit upwards and sideways, out of the way, instead of letting it slide under the wheels and derail the train. The British mathematician Charles Babbage had suggested a similar device in England, but Dripps is usually credited with the first practical one, in 1833.

Other American features followed. Trains often ran through the night across dark countryside, so locomotives gained big headlamps at the front, at first burning oil and later lit by electricity. Large brass bells on top of the boiler, along with steam whistles, warned people and animals at the many level crossings where roads crossed the tracks with no gates. Over time the John Bull itself was given a cab to shelter the crew, a bell and a headlight.

Because America had vast forests and, in many places, little coal, early American engines often burned wood. Burning wood throws out showers of glowing sparks that could set fields and forests on fire, so many American locomotives wore huge balloon-shaped or funnel-shaped chimneys containing screens to catch the sparks. Put all these features together, the pilot, the swivelling truck, the bell, the big lamp and the fat chimney, and you have the classic look of an American locomotive from cowboy films. By the 1850s the most common design was called the American type, with four small wheels in front and four large driving wheels behind. It was simple, sturdy and flexible, and thousands were built.

The results were spectacular. By 1840 the United States had roughly 3,000 miles of railroad, by most counts more than all of Europe combined, and by 1860 it had around 30,000 miles. Railroads stitched together towns and farms, especially in the North and the Midwest, and cities like Chicago grew at astonishing speed as railway lines met there. But those same rails were about to be tested in the most terrible way of all.

sections.heading: Rails at War
paragraphs: In April 1861 the American Civil War began. Eleven Southern states had broken away to form the Confederacy, largely to protect slavery, and the Northern states, the Union, fought to bring them back. It was the first major war in which railways played a central part, and generals on both sides quickly learned that whoever controlled the tracks could move soldiers and food faster than the enemy could march.

Here the North had a huge advantage. Historians usually estimate that in 1861 the Northern states had roughly 22,000 miles of railroad, while the Southern states had only about 9,000. The North also had most of the factories that made rails and locomotives. Southern railroads had mostly been built for short hauls, carrying cotton from plantations to the nearest river or port, and many of them did not even join up with each other. Some used different track gauges, so in certain towns cargo had to be unloaded from one train, carried across the streets by horse and cart, and loaded onto another. When Southern locomotives wore out, there were few workshops to repair them or build new ones, and by the last year of the war the Confederate railroad system was close to collapse.

Early in 1862 the US Congress gave President Abraham Lincoln the power to take over railroads and telegraph lines for military use, and the government created the United States Military Railroad. It was run by Daniel McCallum, a former manager of the Erie Railroad, while a brilliant engineer from the Pennsylvania Railroad, Herman Haupt, took charge of construction and repairs in Virginia. Haupt's crews became famous for rebuilding wrecked bridges in days using timber cut from nearby forests. When the war began, the Military Railroad ran just 7 miles of line; by the end it controlled more than 2,000 miles and had bought, built or captured over 400 locomotives.

Armies also used trains to move troops astonishing distances. In autumn 1863, after a Union defeat at Chickamauga in Georgia, more than 20,000 Union soldiers were rushed by rail from Virginia to the area around Chattanooga, a journey of about 1,200 miles (about 2,000 km) completed in under two weeks. Marching that far would have taken months.

Because railroads were so valuable, they became targets. Soldiers tore up track, burned bridges and wrecked engines. Union troops in Georgia heated rails over bonfires and twisted them around tree trunks so they could never be reused; people called them 'Sherman's neckties', after General William T. Sherman. One of the war's most exciting episodes was the Great Locomotive Chase of 12 April 1862. A band of Union volunteers led by a civilian scout named James Andrews stole a Confederate locomotive called the General in northern Georgia and raced north, trying to wreck the line behind them. The train's conductor, William Fuller, chased them on foot, then on a handcar, then on a series of locomotives, finally steaming backwards in an engine called the Texas. After about 87 miles (140 km) the General ran out of fuel and the raiders fled into the woods. All of them were captured within about two weeks, and Andrews and several others were executed. Some of the survivors became the very first people ever awarded the US Medal of Honor. The General and the Texas both survive in museums in Georgia today.

sections.heading: The Underground Railroad: A Railroad That Wasn't
paragraphs: Before and during these years, Americans talked about another 'railroad', and it is important to be very clear about it. The Underground Railroad was NOT a real railway. It had no tracks, no tunnels and no locomotives. It was a secret network of brave people, Black and white, free and formerly enslaved, who helped enslaved people escape from the Southern states to freedom in the North, in Canada, and sometimes in Mexico or the Caribbean.

The name appeared in print in 1842 and became popular in the 1840s, just as real railroads were the most exciting new thing in the country. The man who first printed it, an abolitionist named Thomas Smallwood, said it came from a Baltimore constable who joked that escapers vanished so completely they must have travelled by 'underground rail-road'. Whatever its exact origin, the idea caught on, because railway words made a perfect secret code. People who guided escapers were called 'conductors'. Safe houses where they could hide, eat and rest were 'stations' or 'depots', and the people who ran them were 'station masters' or 'stationmasters'. The escaping people themselves were sometimes called 'passengers' or 'cargo'. Canada, where slavery was illegal, was nicknamed the 'Promised Land', and the Ohio River, the border between slave states and free states, was the 'River Jordan'.

Most freedom seekers travelled on foot, often at night, following rivers or the North Star, hiding in barns, cellars, attics and swamps. The most famous conductor was Harriet Tubman, who escaped from slavery in Maryland herself and then went back about 13 times, leading around 70 people, including members of her own family, to freedom. In Philadelphia, a free Black man named William Still helped hundreds of people and secretly kept careful records of their stories, which he later published in 1872.

Sometimes real trains did play a part. In September 1838 a young man named Frederick Douglass escaped from slavery in Baltimore by boarding a northbound train, dressed in a sailor's uniform and carrying papers borrowed from a free Black sailor. With the help of Anna Murray, the free woman he would soon marry, he reached New York in less than a day. He went on to become one of the greatest speakers and writers in American history.

Nobody knows exactly how many people escaped this way, because the whole network depended on secrecy. One estimate suggests around 100,000 people had escaped by 1850. Escaping became even more dangerous after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, which forced officials in free states to help catch escapers, and many freedom seekers then pushed on all the way to Canada. The Underground Railroad borrowed the language of the railway age, but its engine was courage.

sections.heading: A Railroad to the Pacific
paragraphs: By the 1850s America stretched all the way to the Pacific Ocean. California had joined the United States in 1850, just after the Gold Rush brought tens of thousands of fortune-seekers west. But getting there was an ordeal. Travellers could spend four to six months bumping across plains, deserts and mountains in a covered wagon, or sail for months around the tip of South America, or take a ship to Panama, cross its jungles and catch another ship north. Many people dreamed of a Pacific railroad that would join the two coasts.

The problem was not just mountains. It was politics. In 1853 Congress paid for army surveys of several possible routes, but Northern and Southern politicians could not agree. A Northern route would help Northern cities and spread free states westward; a Southern route would help the South and might spread slavery. Year after year, the arguments went nowhere.

The Civil War broke that deadlock. When the Southern states left the Union, their members of Congress left too, and the remaining lawmakers could choose a central route. On 1 July 1862, in the middle of the war, President Abraham Lincoln signed the Pacific Railway Act. Lincoln had worked as a lawyer for railroad companies in Illinois before becoming president, and he strongly believed a railroad would help hold the country together.

The Act gave the job to two companies. The Central Pacific Railroad, already set up in California, would build eastward from Sacramento. A brand new company, the Union Pacific Railroad, would build westward from the Missouri River. Because nobody would risk building through empty plains and mountains without help, the government offered huge rewards. For every mile of track, each company received grants of public land in a checkerboard pattern on both sides of the line, about 6,400 acres per mile, which it could sell to settlers. It also received government bonds, a kind of loan, worth $16,000 for every mile on flat ground, $32,000 in the hilly country and $48,000 per mile in the high mountains. Of course, that land was not really empty. It was home to many Native American nations, a part of the story we will face honestly in the next chapter.

So the stage was set for one of the greatest building contests in history. On one side, in California, a company whose route led straight into the granite walls of the Sierra Nevada. On the other, far away on the banks of the Missouri River near Omaha, a company facing a thousand miles of open plains and the Rocky Mountains beyond. Each was paid by the mile, so each wanted to build as fast as it possibly could. Two railroads, one starting in California and one on the Missouri River, were about to race towards each other to meet somewhere in the middle.

deepDive: Why did American railways look and behave so differently from British ones? Economic historians point to the price of things. In Britain, land and labour were expensive but capital (money for investment) was relatively plentiful, so engineers built for the long term: heavy rails, gentle curves, solid stone viaducts and long tunnels, paid for up front. In the United States the situation was reversed. Land and timber were cheap, skilled labour and capital were scarce, and distances were vast. It made sense to build quickly and cheaply, accept sharp curves and steep grades, and improve the line later once traffic paid for it. That choice shaped the machines. Swivelling leading trucks (Jervis, 1832), equalising levers that spread weight across wheels on uneven track, and the flexible 4-4-0 American type were all answers to poor track rather than ideal track. Historians also debate how important railroads really were to American growth. In 1964 the economist Robert Fogel famously argued that if the US had never built railroads and had relied on canals and wagons instead, its national income in 1890 would have been only a few percent lower. His 'counterfactual' method was hugely influential and helped win him a share of the 1993 Nobel Prize in economics, but many historians replied that railroads also changed things that are hard to measure: where cities grew, how businesses were organised, and how fast people and information could move. The Civil War offers another debate. The North's roughly 22,000 miles of track versus the South's roughly 9,000 are often quoted, but historians stress that quality mattered as much as quantity. Southern lines used several gauges, were poorly connected, and depended on Northern or foreign factories for rails and engines. Once the blockade cut off imports, the South could not replace worn-out equipment, while Union railroad managers such as Daniel McCallum pioneered organised timetables, repair crews and chains of command that later influenced how large American corporations were run. Finally, a note on 'firsts': the Baltimore and Ohio is often called America's first common-carrier railroad (open to anyone who paid), the Best Friend of Charleston ran the first scheduled steam passenger service, and the Stourbridge Lion made one of the first locomotive runs. Each claim is true in its own carefully worded way.
funFact: The first stone of the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad was laid on 4 July 1828 with the help of Charles Carroll, who had signed the Declaration of Independence 52 years earlier.

check.q: Why did Peter Cooper's Tom Thumb lose its 1830 race against a horse?
check.a: The belt driving its fire blower slipped off, so the engine lost power
wrong: It ran out of water in the first mile
The horse took a shortcut across a field
A cow wandered onto the track and blocked it
